1→# Optimizing Rust Binaries with build-std
     2→
     3→## 20260119 - Key Finding
     4→
     5→Rust binaries using std can be dramatically reduced using nightly's `build-std` feature with `panic=immediate-abort`:
     6→
     7→| Target | Baseline | Optimized | Reduction |
     8→|--------|----------|-----------|-----------|
     9→| glibc (dynamic) | ~298 KB | ~9 KB | 97% |
    10→| musl (static) | ~381 KB | ~23 KB | 94% |
    11→| x2 (rlibc-x2) | ~41 KB | ~6 KB | 85% |
    12→
    13→**The bloat isn't libc - it's Rust's panic formatting machinery.**
    14→
    15→### Why This Works
    16→
    17→#### The Real Win: Eliminating Panic Machinery
    18→
    19→Both glibc and musl baselines have ~280-340 KB of text. That's almost entirely `core::fmt` infrastructure for panic messages. Standard panic handlers pull in formatting code, which brings in large portions of the formatting machinery.
    20→
    21→Using `-C panic=immediate-abort` with `-Z build-std` rebuilds the standard library to immediately abort on panic without any formatting.
    22→
    23→#### Dynamic vs Static After Optimization
    24→
    25→- **glibc (dynamic, 9.3 KB)** is smaller than **musl (static, 22.7 KB)**
    26→- Makes sense: musl code is embedded in the binary, glibc code lives in system's `libc.so.6`
    27→- Both achieve massive reductions because the optimization targets Rust's std, not the libc
    28→
    29→#### Musl Already Uses Function Sections
    30→
    31→The musl `libc.a` bundled with Rust is compiled with `-ffunction-sections -fdata-sections`:
    32→
    33→```
    34→$ ar x libc.a exit.lo
    35→$ readelf -S exit.lo | grep .text
    36→  [ 5] .text.libc_e[...] PROGBITS  ...  # .text.libc_exit_fini
    37→  [ 7] .text.exit        PROGBITS  ...
    38→```
    39→
    40→This enables `--gc-sections` to remove unused functions, though LTO already handles most dead code elimination.
    41→
    42→#### Why rlibc-x2 is Still Smaller
    43→
    44→Even with full optimization:
    45→- ex-x2 (rlibc-x2): 6.4 KB
    46→- ex-glibc: 9.3 KB
    47→- ex-musl: 22.7 KB
    48→
    49→rlibc-x2 is purpose-built to be minimal, while glibc/musl are complete, production-ready implementations with more infrastructure.
    50→
    51→### Manual Commands
    52→
    53→If not using xtask, here are the raw cargo commands:
    54→
    55→#### For glibc (dynamic linking)
    56→
    57→```bash
    58→RUSTFLAGS="-Z unstable-options -C panic=immediate-abort" \
    59→  cargo +nightly build --release \
    60→  --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu \
    61→  -Z build-std=std,core,panic_abort
    62→strip target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/<binary>
    63→```
    64→
    65→#### For musl (static linking)
    66→
    67→```bash
    68→RUSTFLAGS="-Z unstable-options -C panic=immediate-abort" \
    69→  cargo +nightly build --release \
    70→  --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl \
    71→  -Z build-std=std,core,panic_abort
    72→strip target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/<binary>
    73→```
    74→
    75→### API Change Note
    76→
    77→The `panic_immediate_abort` feature changed in recent nightly Rust. It's now a proper panic strategy:
    78→
    79→**Old (no longer works):**
    80→```bash
    81→-Z build-std-features=panic_immediate_abort
    82→```
    83→
    84→**New:**
    85→```bash
    86→RUSTFLAGS="-Z unstable-options -C panic=immediate-abort"
    87→```
    88→
    89→### Requirements
    90→
    91→- Rust nightly toolchain
    92→- `rust-src` component: `rustup component add rust-src --toolchain nightly`
    93→- For musl: `rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`
    94→
    95→## 20260120 - Extended -opt to all apps
    96→
    97→### Size Comparison
    98→
    99→All apps built with `cargo xtask build <app> -r -opt -s`:
   100→
   101→| App | Runtime | Stable | Nightly | Description |
   102→|-----|---------|-------:|--------:|-------------|
   103→| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | 1.4 KB | - | Exit-only (no_std) |
   104→| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | 1.6 KB | - | Hello world (no_std) |
   105→| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | 41 KB | 6.4 KB | Exit-only (std) |
   106→| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | 46 KB | 8.9 KB | Hello world (std) |
   107→| ex-glibc | glibc | 298 KB | 9.3 KB | Exit-only (dynamic) |
   108→| hw-glibc | glibc | 287 KB | 11.9 KB | Hello world (dynamic) |
   109→| ex-musl | musl | 381 KB | 22.7 KB | Exit-only (static) |
   110→| hw-musl | musl | 377 KB | 26.8 KB | Hello world (static) |
   111→
   112→The `-x1` apps don't benefit from `-opt` since they're already `no_std`.
   113→
   114→### Using xtask
   115→
   116→The `-opt` flag in xtask enables these optimizations for x2, glibc, and musl crates:
   117→
   118→```bash
   119→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -opt -s     # rlibc-x2 based
   120→cargo xtask build ex-glibc -r -opt -s  # glibc (dynamic)
   121→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt -s   # musl (static)
   122→cargo xtask build hw-glibc -r -opt -s  # hello world variants too
   123→```
   124→
   125→The `-x1` crates are already `no_std`, so `-opt` has no effect on them.
   126→
   127→## 20260120 - Preserving Symbols for Analysis
   128→
   129→### The Problem
   130→
   131→When using `-Z build-std`, the `.symtab` section was being stripped even with `strip = false` in Cargo.toml. This made `func-analysis` unable to show app function sizes for optimized builds.
   132→
   133→### The Solution
   134→
   135→Use the explicit string form `strip = "none"` in Cargo.toml:
   136→
   137→```toml
   138→[profile.release]
   139→strip = "none"    # Preserves .symtab for analysis
   140→```
   141→
   142→This ensures symbols survive the build-std + LTO pipeline.
   143→
   144→### Workflow
   145→
   146→Two build modes for different purposes:
   147→
   148→```bash
   149→# For analysis - preserves symbols
   150→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt
   151→func-analysis analyze target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/ex-musl
   152→
   153→# For production - strips symbols, smallest size
   154→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt -s
   155→```
   156→
   157→### func-analysis Output
   158→
   159→With symbols preserved, `func-analysis` shows both app and library functions:
   160→
   161→**Static binaries (musl, x2):** Shows local Rust functions + embedded libc functions
   162→```
   163→Functions: 73
   164→Functions size: 9215 bytes
   165→.text size: 9357 bytes
   166→Coverage: 98.5%
   167→```
   168→
   169→**Dynamic binaries (glibc):** Shows local Rust functions + imported libc functions (sizes from system libc)
   170→```
   171→Functions: 38
   172→Functions size: 7284 bytes
   173→.text size: 2470 bytes
   174→Coverage: 294.9%   # >100% because libc sizes are external
   175→```
   176→
   177→### Why Coverage Can Exceed 100%
   178→
   179→For dynamic binaries, "Functions size" sums both:
   180→- Local function sizes (from the binary's `.symtab`)
   181→- Imported libc function sizes (from system's `libc.so.6`)
   182→
   183→But `.text size` only measures local code, so coverage exceeds 100% when libc function sizes are included.
   184→
   185→## 20260120 - Version Scripts and Dead Code Elimination
   186→
   187→### The Problem
   188→
   189→When building an executable (not a shared library), there's no good reason for internal symbols to be GLOBAL/exported. The only entry point is `_start` - nothing external can call internal functions at runtime. However, the linker keeps GLOBAL symbols by default, preventing `--gc-sections` from removing unreferenced code.
   190→
   191→### The Solution: Version Scripts
   192→
   193→We use a linker "version script" to make all symbols LOCAL except `_start`:
   194→
   195→```
   196→{ global: _start; local: *; };
   197→```
   198→
   199→Combined with `--gc-sections`, this allows the linker to remove unreferenced functions. For ex-x2, this reduced the stripped binary from ~13KB to ~6KB.
   200→
   201→### Why This Is Frustrating
   202→
   203→The linker should have a simple flag like `--executable-hide-symbols` that automatically makes all symbols local except the entry point. This would:
   204→
   205→1. Enable dead code elimination via `--gc-sections`
   206→2. Improve security by hiding internal implementation details
   207→3. Reduce binary size by eliminating `.dynsym` bloat
   208→
   209→Instead, we must create a version script file with arcane syntax. A short-term improvement would be accepting the configuration directly:
   210→
   211→```bash
   212→-Wl,--version-script="{ global: _start; local: *; }"
   213→```
   214→
   215→But this doesn't work - the linker requires an actual file.
   216→
   217→### Current Implementation
   218→
   219→The `-opt` flag in xtask generates `target/opt-version.config` and passes it to the linker:
   220→
   221→```bash
   222→RUSTFLAGS="-C panic=immediate-abort -Z unstable-options \
   223→  -C link-arg=-Wl,--gc-sections \
   224→  -C link-arg=-Wl,--version-script=target/opt-version.config"
   225→```
   226→
   227→### Impact on Real Applications
   228→
   229→For minimal apps (ex-*), the version script provides significant savings. For larger applications like func-analysis, LTO already handles most dead code elimination, so the version script has minimal additional impact:
   230→
   231→| Build | Stripped Size |
   232→|-------|---:|
   233→| `cargo build --release && strip` | 886 KB |
   234→| `cargo xtask build -r -opt -s` | 683 KB |
   235→| **Reduction** | **23%** |
   236→
   237→## 20260120 - Does using -no-pie reduce of a binary
   238→

   240→
   241→```
   242→[profile.release-no-pie]
   243→inherits = "release"
   244→strip = "symbols"
   245→link-args = ["-no-pie"]
   246→```
   247→
   248→The using that didn't change the size
   249→
   250→### Modified xtask/src/main.rs
   251→
   252→Talked with Claude
   253→[claude on no-pie](https://claude.ai/share/508cfeb9-d1bb-4592-97ad-ec468f827f93)
   254→
   255→Added `-C link-args=-no-pie` to rustflags:

   257→            "-C panic=immediate-abort -Z unstable-options -C link-args=-no-pie -C link-arg=-Wl,--gc-sections -C link-arg=-Wl,--version-script={}",
   258→            //"-C panic=immediate-abort -Z unstable-options -C link-arg=-Wl,--gc-sections -C link-arg=-Wl,--version-script={}",
   259→            version_config.display()
   260→        );
   261→
   262→built twice without one with -no-pie and once without, both times using:
   263→```
   264→cargo clean ; cargo xtask build -vc -r -opt -s  func-analysis`
   265→```
   266→And copied them to `fa-r-opt-s` and `fa-r-opt-s-no-pie` see below:
   267→```
   268→wink@3900x 26-01-21T02:38:24.386Z:~/data/prgs/rust/rlibc-x (main)

1→# PLT-less Linking in Modern ELF Binaries
     2→
     3→## 20260120 - Discovery: Optimized glibc binaries use GLOB_DAT instead of PLT
     4→
     5→When building with `-opt` (nightly + build-std + panic=immediate-abort), the linker
     6→produces binaries without a traditional `.plt` section. Instead of:
     7→
     8→```
     9→call printf@plt        ; jump to PLT stub
    10→```
    11→
    12→The binary uses direct GOT calls:
    13→
    14→```
    15→call *0x1b93(%rip)     ; call through GOT entry directly
    16→```
    17→
    18→### Traditional PLT linking
    19→
    20→```
    21→.rela.plt:  R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT relocations
    22→.plt:       PLT stubs (16 bytes each)
    23→.got.plt:   GOT entries for lazy binding
    24→
    25→Code: call <plt_stub> -> plt_stub jumps through GOT
    26→```
    27→
    28→### PLT-less linking (GLOB_DAT)
    29→
    30→```
    31→.rela.dyn:  R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT relocations
    32→.got:       GOT entries (no lazy binding)
    33→No .plt section
    34→
    35→Code: call *offset(%rip) -> direct GOT call
    36→```
    37→
    38→### Why this happens
    39→
    40→The optimized build flags likely trigger the linker to use `-z now` (immediate binding)
    41→which eliminates the need for PLT stubs. The GOT entries are resolved at load time,
    42→so there's no need for the lazy binding infrastructure.
    43→
    44→### Impact on func-analysis
    45→
    46→The `func-analysis` tool needed updates to handle both styles:
    47→
    48→1. `build_plt_map()` now checks `.rela.dyn` for `GLOB_DAT` relocations when no `.plt` exists
    49→2. `extract_call_target()` now resolves RIP-relative indirect calls (`call *offset(%rip)`)
    50→3. Call detection includes `FlowControl::IndirectCall` for indirect calls
    51→
    52→### Verification
    53→
    54→```bash
    55→# Check if binary has .plt section
    56→readelf -S binary | grep '\.plt'
    57→
    58→# Check relocation types
    59→readelf -r binary | grep -E 'JUMP_SLOT|GLOB_DAT'
    60→
    61→# Traditional PLT: JUMP_SLOT in .rela.plt
    62→# PLT-less: GLOB_DAT in .rela.dyn
    63→```
    64→

1→# rlibc-x
     2→
     3→A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→## Goals
     6→
     7→- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
     8→- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
     9→- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`
    10→
    11→## Results
    12→
    13→The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:
    14→
    15→```
    16→$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
    17→-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1
    18→
    19→$ file target/release/ex-x1
    20→ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
    21→```
    22→
    23→This is achieved through:
    24→- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
    25→- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
    26→- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
    27→- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
    28→- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols
    29→
    30→For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces **~6 KB** with `-opt` (nightly).
    31→
    32→See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison.
    33→
    34→## Workspace Structure
    35→
    36→| Directory | Description |
    37→|-----------|-------------|
    38→| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
    39→| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~6-41 KB binaries) |
    40→| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
    41→| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`, `func-analysis`) |
    42→| [notes/](notes/) | Technical notes and findings |
    43→| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |
    44→
    45→## Two Approaches
    46→
    47→**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.
    48→
    49→**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.
    50→
    51→## Optimized Builds
    52→
    53→The `-opt` flag dramatically reduces binary sizes by eliminating Rust's panic formatting machinery:
    54→
    55→```bash
    56→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -opt -s     # ~6 KB (vs ~41 KB)
    57→cargo xtask build ex-glibc -r -opt -s  # ~9 KB (vs ~298 KB)
    58→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt -s   # ~23 KB (vs ~381 KB)
    59→```
    60→
    61→See [notes/opt-notes.md](notes/opt-notes.md) for details.
    62→
    63→## Quick Start
    64→
    65→```bash
    66→# Build and run
    67→cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
    68→cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2
    69→
    70→# Test
    71→cargo xtask test               # run all tests
    72→cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode
    73→
    74→# Build release
    75→cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
    76→```
    77→
    78→For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)
    79→
    80→## Verifying No libc Usage
    81→
    82→The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:
    83→
    84→```bash
    85→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
    86→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
    87→```
    88→
    89→All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.
    90→
    91→## Status
    92→
    93→This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:
    94→
    95→- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
    96→- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust
    97→
    98→## Origin
    99→
   100→Started with this prompt for Claude Code:
   101→
   102→> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
   103→> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
   104→> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
   105→> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."
   106→
   107→Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

    14→
    15→Build crates one at a time.
    16→
    17→```bash
    18→cargo xtask build                 # build all crates
    19→cargo xtask build ex-x1           # build specific crate
    20→cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r        # build with release profile
    21→```
    22→
    23→### run
    24→
    25→Build and run crates, showing exit codes. Library-only crates (no `src/main.rs`) are automatically skipped.
    26→
    27→```bash
    28→cargo xtask run hw-x1             # run specific crate
    29→cargo xtask run .                 # run crate in current directory
    30→cargo xtask run                   # run all binary crates
    31→```
    32→
    33→### test
    34→
    35→Run tests with a summary at the end.
    36→
    37→```bash
    38→cargo xtask test                  # test all crates
    39→cargo xtask test ex-x1            # test specific crate
    40→cargo xtask test rlibc-x2         # also runs rlibc-x2-tests binaries
    41→```
    42→
    43→## Options
    44→
    45→| Option | Description |
    46→|--------|-------------|
    47→| `-q, --quiet` | Suppress cargo output (default is verbose) |
    48→| `-f, --fail-fast` | Stop on first failure |
    49→| `-d, --debug` | Use debug builds (default) |
    50→| `-r, --release` | Use release builds |
    51→| `-opt, --optimized` | Use nightly optimizations (x2, glibc, musl) |
    52→| `-s, --strip` | Strip debug symbols after building |
    53→| `-h, --help` | Show help |
    54→
    55→## Features
    56→
    57→- **One crate at a time**: Each crate is processed individually for clear output
    58→- **Musl auto-detection**: Crates with "musl" in the name use `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`
    59→- **Current directory**: Use `.` to operate on the crate in the current directory
    60→- **Exit codes**: The `run` command shows exit codes for each binary
    61→- **Binary path**: The `build` command shows the path to the built binary
    62→- **Smart stripping**: With `-s`, `run` only strips if the binary was rebuilt (uses mtime)
    63→
    64→## Optimized Builds

1→# rlibc-x1
     2→
     3→A minimal `#![no_std]` runtime for Rust on Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→Produces tiny binaries (~1.4 KB) by eliminating standard library overhead entirely.
     6→
     7→## How It Works
     8→
     9→```
    10→_start (asm) → _start_rust() → main() → exit()
    11→```
    12→
    13→- **`_start`** - Assembly entry point, sets up stack and calls `_start_rust()`
    14→- **`_start_rust()`** - Calls user's `main()` function
    15→- **`main()`** - User-defined, must call `exit()` to terminate
    16→- **`exit()`** - Direct syscall, no glibc
    17→
    18→## Provided Functions
    19→
    20→| Category | Functions |
    21→|----------|-----------|
    22→| Process | `exit()` |
    23→| Memory | `malloc()`, `realloc()`, `free()` (no-op) |
    24→| I/O | `read()`, `write()` |
    25→| Syscalls | `syscall0` through `syscall6` |
    26→
    27→The allocator is a simple bump allocator using `brk()`. Memory is never freed.
    28→
    29→## Usage
    30→
    31→1. Add dependency:
    32→   ```toml
    33→   [dependencies]
    34→   rlibc-x1 = { path = "../rlibc-x1" }
    35→   ```
    36→
    37→2. Configure your app:
    38→   ```rust
    39→   #![no_std]
    40→   #![no_main]
    41→
    42→   #[unsafe(no_mangle)]
    43→   fn main() {
    44→       rlibc_x1::exit(0);
    45→   }
    46→   ```
    47→
    48→3. Add linker flags in `build.rs`:
    49→   ```rust
    50→   fn main() {
    51→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-nostartfiles");
    52→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-static");
    53→   }
    54→   ```
    55→
    56→## Example
    57→
    58→See [apps/ex-x1](../apps/ex-x1) and [apps/hw-x1](../apps/hw-x1) for complete examples.
    59→

1→# rlibc-x2
     2→
     3→A libc replacement that allows using Rust's standard library without linking to glibc.
     4→
     5→Produces statically-linked binaries that use `std` but make no glibc calls:
     6→- **~41 KB** with stable Rust
     7→- **~6 KB** with nightly optimizations
     8→
     9→## How It Works
    10→
    11→```
    12→_start (asm) → __libc_start_main() → Rust's main → user's main()
    13→```
    14→
    15→- **`_start`** - Assembly entry point
    16→- **`__libc_start_main()`** - Initializes TLS, environment, then calls Rust's generated main
    17→- **Rust's main** - Standard library initialization
    18→- **User's `main()`** - Normal Rust main function
    19→
    20→## Provided Symbols
    21→
    22→| Category | Symbols |
    23→|----------|---------|
    24→| Process | `_start`, `__libc_start_main`, `exit`, `abort`, `__libc_stack_end` |
    25→| Environment | `environ`, `getenv` |
    26→| Memory | `malloc`, `realloc`, `calloc`, `free`, `memcpy`, `memset`, `memmove`, `memcmp` |
    27→| I/O | `read`, `write`, `writev` |
    28→| Threading | `pthread_*` stubs, TLS initialization |
    29→| Other | `__errno_location`, signal stubs |
    30→
    31→## Usage
    32→
    33→1. Add dependency:
    34→   ```toml
    35→   [dependencies]
    36→   rlibc-x2 = { path = "../rlibc-x2" }
    37→   ```
    38→
    39→2. Force linking in your app:
    40→   ```rust
    41→   extern crate rlibc_x2;
    42→
    43→   fn main() {
    44→       std::process::exit(42);
    45→   }
    46→   ```
    47→
    48→3. Add linker flags in `build.rs`:
    49→   ```rust
    50→   fn main() {
    51→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-static");
    52→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-nostdlib");
    53→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-nodefaultlibs");
    54→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-e_start");
    55→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-Wl,--undefined=_start");
    56→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-Wl,--undefined=__libc_start_main");
    57→   }
    58→   ```
    59→
    60→## The "Dynamically Linked" Discrepancy
    61→
    62→`file` reports "dynamically linked" but `ldd` says "statically linked" - both are correct:
    63→
    64→- **`file`** sees `.dynamic` and `.dynsym` ELF sections (required by Rust's std)
    65→- **`ldd`** sees no INTERP section, so no dynamic linker is invoked
    66→
    67→Use `strace` to verify - only ~7 syscalls, no library loading.
    68→
    69→## Integration Tests
    70→
    71→Tests are in `tests/` and built as separate binaries:
    72→
    73→```bash
    74→cargo xtask test rlibc-x2    # runs rlibc-x2-tests binaries
    75→```
    76→
    77→## Build Modes
    78→
    79→### Stable (default)
    80→
    81→Works with stable Rust, produces ~41 KB binaries:
    82→
    83→```bash
    84→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -s
    85→```
    86→
    87→### Optimized (nightly)
    88→
    89→Uses nightly features for ~6 KB binaries:
    90→
    91→```bash
    92→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -opt -s
    93→```
    94→
    95→The `-opt` flag enables:
    96→- `-Z build-std` - Rebuild std from source for better LTO
    97→- `-Z panic-immediate-abort` - Eliminate panic formatting code
    98→- Linker version script - Enable dead code elimination
    99→- Custom target - `x86_64-unknown-linux-rlibcx2.json`
   100→
   101→## Example
   102→
   103→See [apps/ex-x2](../apps/ex-x2) and [apps/hw-x2](../apps/hw-x2) for complete examples.
   104→

1→# Optimizing Rust Binaries with build-std
     2→
     3→## 20260119 - Key Finding
     4→
     5→Rust binaries using std can be dramatically reduced using nightly's `build-std` feature with `panic=immediate-abort`:
     6→
     7→| Target | Baseline | Optimized | Reduction |
     8→|--------|----------|-----------|-----------|
     9→| glibc (dynamic) | ~298 KB | ~9 KB | 97% |
    10→| musl (static) | ~381 KB | ~23 KB | 94% |
    11→| x2 (rlibc-x2) | ~41 KB | ~6 KB | 85% |
    12→
    13→**The bloat isn't libc - it's Rust's panic formatting machinery.**
    14→
    15→### Why This Works
    16→
    17→#### The Real Win: Eliminating Panic Machinery
    18→
    19→Both glibc and musl baselines have ~280-340 KB of text. That's almost entirely `core::fmt` infrastructure for panic messages. Standard panic handlers pull in formatting code, which brings in large portions of the formatting machinery.
    20→
    21→Using `-C panic=immediate-abort` with `-Z build-std` rebuilds the standard library to immediately abort on panic without any formatting.
    22→
    23→#### Dynamic vs Static After Optimization
    24→
    25→- **glibc (dynamic, 9.3 KB)** is smaller than **musl (static, 22.7 KB)**
    26→- Makes sense: musl code is embedded in the binary, glibc code lives in system's `libc.so.6`
    27→- Both achieve massive reductions because the optimization targets Rust's std, not the libc
    28→
    29→#### Musl Already Uses Function Sections
    30→
    31→The musl `libc.a` bundled with Rust is compiled with `-ffunction-sections -fdata-sections`:
    32→
    33→```
    34→$ ar x libc.a exit.lo
    35→$ readelf -S exit.lo | grep .text
    36→  [ 5] .text.libc_e[...] PROGBITS  ...  # .text.libc_exit_fini
    37→  [ 7] .text.exit        PROGBITS  ...
    38→```
    39→
    40→This enables `--gc-sections` to remove unused functions, though LTO already handles most dead code elimination.
    41→
    42→#### Why rlibc-x2 is Still Smaller
    43→
    44→Even with full optimization:
    45→- ex-x2 (rlibc-x2): 6.4 KB
    46→- ex-glibc: 9.3 KB
    47→- ex-musl: 22.7 KB
    48→
    49→rlibc-x2 is purpose-built to be minimal, while glibc/musl are complete, production-ready implementations with more infrastructure.
    50→
    51→### Manual Commands
    52→
    53→If not using xtask, here are the raw cargo commands:
    54→
    55→#### For glibc (dynamic linking)
    56→
    57→```bash
    58→RUSTFLAGS="-Z unstable-options -C panic=immediate-abort" \
    59→  cargo +nightly build --release \
    60→  --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu \
    61→  -Z build-std=std,core,panic_abort
    62→strip target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/<binary>
    63→```
    64→
    65→#### For musl (static linking)
    66→
    67→```bash
    68→RUSTFLAGS="-Z unstable-options -C panic=immediate-abort" \
    69→  cargo +nightly build --release \
    70→  --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl \
    71→  -Z build-std=std,core,panic_abort
    72→strip target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/<binary>
    73→```
    74→
    75→### API Change Note
    76→
    77→The `panic_immediate_abort` feature changed in recent nightly Rust. It's now a proper panic strategy:
    78→
    79→**Old (no longer works):**
    80→```bash
    81→-Z build-std-features=panic_immediate_abort
    82→```
    83→
    84→**New:**
    85→```bash
    86→RUSTFLAGS="-Z unstable-options -C panic=immediate-abort"
    87→```
    88→
    89→### Requirements
    90→
    91→- Rust nightly toolchain
    92→- `rust-src` component: `rustup component add rust-src --toolchain nightly`
    93→- For musl: `rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`
    94→
    95→## 20260120 - Extended -opt to all apps
    96→
    97→### Size Comparison
    98→
    99→All apps built with `cargo xtask build <app> -r -opt -s`:
   100→
   101→| App | Runtime | Stable | Nightly | Description |
   102→|-----|---------|-------:|--------:|-------------|
   103→| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | 1.4 KB | - | Exit-only (no_std) |
   104→| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | 1.6 KB | - | Hello world (no_std) |
   105→| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | 41 KB | 6.4 KB | Exit-only (std) |
   106→| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | 46 KB | 8.9 KB | Hello world (std) |
   107→| ex-glibc | glibc | 298 KB | 9.3 KB | Exit-only (dynamic) |
   108→| hw-glibc | glibc | 287 KB | 11.9 KB | Hello world (dynamic) |
   109→| ex-musl | musl | 381 KB | 22.7 KB | Exit-only (static) |
   110→| hw-musl | musl | 377 KB | 26.8 KB | Hello world (static) |
   111→
   112→The `-x1` apps don't benefit from `-opt` since they're already `no_std`.
   113→
   114→### Using xtask
   115→
   116→The `-opt` flag in xtask enables these optimizations for x2, glibc, and musl crates:
   117→
   118→```bash
   119→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -opt -s     # rlibc-x2 based
   120→cargo xtask build ex-glibc -r -opt -s  # glibc (dynamic)
   121→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt -s   # musl (static)
   122→cargo xtask build hw-glibc -r -opt -s  # hello world variants too
   123→```
   124→
   125→The `-x1` crates are already `no_std`, so `-opt` has no effect on them.
   126→
   127→## 20260120 - Preserving Symbols for Analysis
   128→
   129→### The Problem
   130→
   131→When using `-Z build-std`, the `.symtab` section was being stripped even with `strip = false` in Cargo.toml. This made `func-analysis` unable to show app function sizes for optimized builds.
   132→
   133→### The Solution
   134→
   135→Use the explicit string form `strip = "none"` in Cargo.toml:
   136→
   137→```toml
   138→[profile.release]
   139→strip = "none"    # Preserves .symtab for analysis
   140→```
   141→
   142→This ensures symbols survive the build-std + LTO pipeline.
   143→
   144→### Workflow
   145→
   146→Two build modes for different purposes:
   147→
   148→```bash
   149→# For analysis - preserves symbols
   150→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt
   151→func-analysis analyze target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/ex-musl
   152→
   153→# For production - strips symbols, smallest size
   154→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt -s
   155→```
   156→
   157→### func-analysis Output
   158→
   159→With symbols preserved, `func-analysis` shows both app and library functions:
   160→
   161→**Static binaries (musl, x2):** Shows local Rust functions + embedded libc functions
   162→```
   163→Functions: 73
   164→Functions size: 9215 bytes
   165→.text size: 9357 bytes
   166→Coverage: 98.5%
   167→```
   168→
   169→**Dynamic binaries (glibc):** Shows local Rust functions + imported libc functions (sizes from system libc)
   170→```
   171→Functions: 38
   172→Functions size: 7284 bytes
   173→.text size: 2470 bytes
   174→Coverage: 294.9%   # >100% because libc sizes are external
   175→```
   176→
   177→### Why Coverage Can Exceed 100%
   178→
   179→For dynamic binaries, "Functions size" sums both:
   180→- Local function sizes (from the binary's `.symtab`)
   181→- Imported libc function sizes (from system's `libc.so.6`)
   182→
   183→But `.text size` only measures local code, so coverage exceeds 100% when libc function sizes are included.
   184→
   185→## 20260120 - Version Scripts and Dead Code Elimination
   186→
   187→### The Problem
   188→
   189→When building an executable (not a shared library), there's no good reason for internal symbols to be GLOBAL/exported. The only entry point is `_start` - nothing external can call internal functions at runtime. However, the linker keeps GLOBAL symbols by default, preventing `--gc-sections` from removing unreferenced code.
   190→
   191→### The Solution: Version Scripts
   192→
   193→We use a linker "version script" to make all symbols LOCAL except `_start`:
   194→
   195→```
   196→{ global: _start; local: *; };
   197→```
   198→
   199→Combined with `--gc-sections`, this allows the linker to remove unreferenced functions. For ex-x2, this reduced the stripped binary from ~13KB to ~6KB.
   200→
   201→### Why This Is Frustrating
   202→
   203→The linker should have a simple flag like `--executable-hide-symbols` that automatically makes all symbols local except the entry point. This would:
   204→
   205→1. Enable dead code elimination via `--gc-sections`
   206→2. Improve security by hiding internal implementation details
   207→3. Reduce binary size by eliminating `.dynsym` bloat
   208→
   209→Instead, we must create a version script file with arcane syntax. A short-term improvement would be accepting the configuration directly:
   210→
   211→```bash
   212→-Wl,--version-script="{ global: _start; local: *; }"
   213→```
   214→
   215→But this doesn't work - the linker requires an actual file.
   216→
   217→### Current Implementation
   218→
   219→The `-opt` flag in xtask generates `target/opt-version.config` and passes it to the linker:
   220→
   221→```bash
   222→RUSTFLAGS="-C panic=immediate-abort -Z unstable-options \
   223→  -C link-arg=-Wl,--gc-sections \
   224→  -C link-arg=-Wl,--version-script=target/opt-version.config"
   225→```
   226→
   227→### Impact on Real Applications
   228→
   229→For minimal apps (ex-*), the version script provides significant savings. For larger applications like func-analysis, LTO already handles most dead code elimination, so the version script has minimal additional impact:
   230→
   231→| Build | Stripped Size |
   232→|-------|---:|
   233→| `cargo build --release && strip` | 886 KB |
   234→| `cargo xtask build -r -opt -s` | 683 KB |
   235→| **Reduction** | **23%** |
   236→
   237→## 20260120 - Does using -no-pie reduce of a binary
   238→
   239→### I tried adding `profile.release-no-pie`
   240→
   241→```
   242→[profile.release-no-pie]
   243→inherits = "release"
   244→strip = "symbols"
   245→link-args = ["-no-pie"]
   246→```
   247→
   248→The using that didn't change the size
   249→
   250→### Modified xtask/src/main.rs
   251→
   252→Talked with Claude
   253→[claude on no-pie](https://claude.ai/share/508cfeb9-d1bb-4592-97ad-ec468f827f93)
   254→
   255→Added `-C link-args=-no-pie` to rustflags:
   256→        let rustflags = format!(
   257→            "-C panic=immediate-abort -Z unstable-options -C link-args=-no-pie -C link-arg=-Wl,--gc-sections -C link-arg=-Wl,--version-script={}",
   258→            //"-C panic=immediate-abort -Z unstable-options -C link-arg=-Wl,--gc-sections -C link-arg=-Wl,--version-script={}",
   259→            version_config.display()
   260→        );
   261→
   262→built twice without one with -no-pie and once without, both times using:
   263→```
   264→cargo clean ; cargo xtask build -vc -r -opt -s  func-analysis`
   265→```
   266→And copied them to `fa-r-opt-s` and `fa-r-opt-s-no-pie` see below:

1→# PLT-less Linking in Modern ELF Binaries
     2→
     3→## 20260120 - Discovery: Optimized glibc binaries use GLOB_DAT instead of PLT
     4→
     5→When building with `-opt` (nightly + build-std + panic=immediate-abort), the linker
     6→produces binaries without a traditional `.plt` section. Instead of:
     7→
     8→```
     9→call printf@plt        ; jump to PLT stub
    10→```
    11→
    12→The binary uses direct GOT calls:
    13→
    14→```
    15→call *0x1b93(%rip)     ; call through GOT entry directly
    16→```
    17→
    18→### Traditional PLT linking
    19→
    20→```
    21→.rela.plt:  R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT relocations
    22→.plt:       PLT stubs (16 bytes each)
    23→.got.plt:   GOT entries for lazy binding
    24→
    25→Code: call <plt_stub> -> plt_stub jumps through GOT
    26→```
    27→
    28→### PLT-less linking (GLOB_DAT)
    29→
    30→```
    31→.rela.dyn:  R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT relocations
    32→.got:       GOT entries (no lazy binding)
    33→No .plt section
    34→
    35→Code: call *offset(%rip) -> direct GOT call
    36→```
    37→
    38→### Why this happens
    39→
    40→The optimized build flags likely trigger the linker to use `-z now` (immediate binding)
    41→which eliminates the need for PLT stubs. The GOT entries are resolved at load time,
    42→so there's no need for the lazy binding infrastructure.
    43→
    44→### Impact on func-analysis
    45→
    46→The `func-analysis` tool needed updates to handle both styles:
    47→
    48→1. `build_plt_map()` now checks `.rela.dyn` for `GLOB_DAT` relocations when no `.plt` exists
    49→2. `extract_call_target()` now resolves RIP-relative indirect calls (`call *offset(%rip)`)
    50→3. Call detection includes `FlowControl::IndirectCall` for indirect calls
    51→
    52→### Verification
    53→
    54→```bash
    55→# Check if binary has .plt section
    56→readelf -S binary | grep '\.plt'
    57→
    58→# Check relocation types
    59→readelf -r binary | grep -E 'JUMP_SLOT|GLOB_DAT'
    60→
    61→# Traditional PLT: JUMP_SLOT in .rela.plt
    62→# PLT-less: GLOB_DAT in .rela.dyn
    63→```
    64→

Perfect! Now I have a comprehensive understanding of the codebase. Let me compile all this information into a detailed report that captures the architecture and structure for future Claude Code instances.

## Comprehensive Codebase Analysis Report

### Project Overview

**rlibc-x** is an experimental, educational Rust project that implements a minimal libc replacement for Linux x86_64. The primary goals are:

1. **Educational** - Understanding how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
2. **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler libc implementations can produce smaller binaries
3. **Future transparency** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

The project demonstrates achieving **1,480 byte** statically-linked executables using the no_std approach, and **~6 KB** with the std-compatible approach using nightly optimizations.

### Project Structure

The workspace contains 17 crates organized into these categories:

**Core Runtime Libraries:**
- `rlibc-x1` - `#![no_std]` minimal runtime (~1.4 KB binaries)
- `rlibc-x2` - std-compatible libc replacement (~6-41 KB binaries)

**Example Applications (8 total):**
- `apps/ex-x1` and `apps/hw-x1` - rlibc-x1 examples (exit-only and hello world)
- `apps/ex-x2` and `apps/hw-x2` - rlibc-x2 examples (exit-only and hello world)
- `apps/ex-glibc` and `apps/hw-glibc` - glibc comparison examples (dynamic linking)
- `apps/ex-musl` and `apps/hw-musl` - musl comparison examples (static linking)

**Development Tools:**
- `tools/func-analysis` - Analyzes libc function sizes and references in ELF binaries (uses goblin, iced-x86)
- `tools/is-libc-used` - Checks if a binary uses libc (uses object crate)

**Project Automation:**
- `xtask` - Custom build task runner (implements pattern from matklad's cargo-xtask)
- `rlibc-x2/tests` - Integration tests for rlibc-x2

**Configuration Files:**
- `Cargo.toml` - Workspace definition with 17 members
- `rust-toolchain.toml` - Stable channel with rustfmt and clippy
- `x86_64-unknown-linux-rlibcx2.json` - Custom target file for rlibc-x2 (plt-by-default: false)
- `Cargo.lock` - Dependency lock file

### Key Architecture Patterns

#### rlibc-x1 (no_std approach)

**Execution Flow:**
```
_start (asm) → _start_rust() → main() → exit()
```

**Key Features:**
- No standard library overhead
- Direct syscalls using inline x86_64 assembly
- Bump allocator using `brk()` syscall
- `panic="abort"` to eliminate unwinding machinery
- `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]` required in applications

**Provided Functions:**
- Process: `exit()`
- Memory: `malloc()`, `realloc()`, `free()` (no-op)
- I/O: `read()`, `write()`
- Syscalls: `syscall0()` through `syscall6()`

**Source Organization (rlibc-x1/src/lib.rs):**
- ~7.9 KB single file containing all functionality
- Direct syscall wrappers
- Memory management with bump allocator
- Panic handler

#### rlibc-x2 (std-compatible approach)

**Execution Flow:**
```
_start (asm) → __libc_start_main() → Rust's main → user's main()
```

**Key Features:**
- Supports Rust std library without glibc
- Statically linked but with ELF dynamic symbols (file reports "dynamically linked" but ldd says "statically linked")
- Integration with Rust's TLS initialization
- Full environment variable support

**Source Organization (rlibc-x2/src/):**
- `lib.rs` - Main entry point and re-exports
- `process.rs` - `_start`, `__libc_start_main`, `exit`, `abort`, `__libc_stack_end`
- `environ.rs` - `environ`, `getenv`, environment handling
- `memory.rs` - `malloc`, `realloc`, `calloc`, `free`, `memcpy`, `memset`, `memmove`, `memcmp`
- `io.rs` - `read`, `write`, `writev`
- `syscall.rs` - Low-level syscall wrappers
- `thread.rs` - pthread stubs and TLS initialization
- `errno.rs` - `__errno_location`
- `signal.rs` - Signal handling stubs

**Linker Flags Required:**
```rust
println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-static");
println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-nostdlib");
println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-nodefaultlibs");
println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-e_start");
println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-Wl,--undefined=_start");
println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-Wl,--undefined=__libc_start_main");
```

### Build System

#### Cargo Configuration

**Profiles:**
```toml
[profile.dev]
panic = "abort"  # Required for rlibc-x1 as it's no-std

[profile.release]
panic = "abort"
opt-level = 'z'      # Size optimization
lto = true           # Link-time optimization
codegen-units = 1    # Better LTO
debug = 2            # Preserve symbols for analysis
debug-assertions = false
overflow-checks = false
incremental = false
strip = "none"       # Preserve .symtab for func-analysis

[profile.release-strip]
inherits = "release"
strip = "symbols"
```

#### xtask Commands

**xtask** is the primary build automation tool. Edition: 2024 (latest).

**Key Commands:**

```bash

- Requires linker flags set in `build.rs` (static, nostdlib, entry point)

### Workspace Structure

```
rlibc-x1/           # no_std runtime library
rlibc-x2/           # std-compatible runtime library
  tests/            # Integration tests (separate binaries)
apps/               # Example applications
  ex-x1, hw-x1      # rlibc-x1 examples (exit-only, hello world)
  ex-x2, hw-x2      # rlibc-x2 examples
  ex-glibc, hw-glibc  # glibc comparison (dynamic)
  ex-musl, hw-musl    # musl comparison (static)
tools/
  func-analysis/    # ELF function size analyzer (goblin, iced-x86)
  is-libc-used/     # Binary libc detection (object crate)
xtask/              # Build automation
notes/              # Technical documentation (opt-notes.md, plt-less-linking.md)
```

### Key Insight: Binary Size

Rust's panic formatting machinery is the primary source of binary bloat, not libc itself. The `-opt` flag achieves 85-97% size reduction by:
- Rebuilding std with `-Z build-std=std,core,panic_abort`
- Using `-C panic=immediate-abort` to eliminate panic formatting
- Version script to make symbols LOCAL, enabling dead code elimination

## Testing

Tests verify that binaries don't use libc and execute correctly:
```bash
cargo xtask test           # All crates
cargo xtask test rlibc-x2  # Includes rlibc-x2-tests binaries
cargo xtask test ex-x1     # Single crate
```

## Conventions

- **Rust Edition:** 2024 for main crates
- **Toolchain:** Stable (nightly only for `-opt` builds)
- **Commit style:** Conventional commits (feat:, docs:, refactor:)
- Apps with "musl" in name auto-target `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`
- Custom target file: `x86_64-unknown-linux-rlibcx2.json` (plt-by-default: false)

Interesting direction. Let me share some thoughts on the design space.

**Current constraints worth noting:**

1. Apps are currently coupled to their runtime at the code level - rlibc-x1 apps need `#![no_std]`/`#![no_main]`, while rlibc-x2/glibc/musl apps use standard Rust
2. Linker flags live in each crate's `build.rs`
3. The `-opt` workflow has multiple moving parts (build-std, version scripts, custom RUSTFLAGS)

**Possible directions:**

**A. Unified "hello world" with conditional compilation**
```rust
// Single hw crate with features
#[cfg(feature = "rlibc-x1")]
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "C" fn main() -> ! { ... }

#[cfg(not(feature = "rlibc-x1"))]
fn main() { ... }
```
Then xtask could build one app against multiple targets. Downside: the code becomes harder to read as a teaching example.

**B. Build profile registry in xtask**
Define target profiles centrally:
```rust
struct TargetProfile {
    triple: Option<&str>,           // None = host
    rustflags: Vec<&str>,
    linker_args: Vec<&str>,
    build_std: Option<&str>,        // e.g., "std,core,panic_abort"
    requires_nightly: bool,
}
```
Then: `cargo xtask build hw-x2 --profile minimal,optimized,debug` to compare the same app with different compilation strategies.

**C. Comparison-focused matrix command**
```bash
cargo xtask compare hw     # builds hw-x1, hw-x2, hw-glibc, hw-musl
cargo xtask compare --all  # full matrix
```
Outputs a table like your README already has, but generated fresh.

**D. External config file (xtask.toml)**
Move target/profile definitions out of code entirely. More flexible but adds another file to maintain.

**My take:** Option B or C seems most aligned with the project's educational goals - you want to compare approaches, not hide the differences. The current separate-app structure is actually good for teaching because each app is a clean, readable example.

# xt Design Notes

Design exploration for `xt` - a translation spec based build system to replace/complement `xtask`.

## Goals

- Compare different target triples and compile/linker commands across multiple apps
- Reproducible builds with fair comparisons
- Explore possibilities by trying specs and recording results
- Type-safe parameter specification leveraging Rust's type system

## Core Concepts

### Translation Specs (tspec)

Two-level specification system:

1. **Global specs** (`tspec/*.toml`) - Define compilation strategies
2. **Local config** (`<crate>/tspec/config.toml`) - Crate compatibility and local modifications

### Directory Structure

```
tspec/                              # Global translation specs
  musl-static.toml
  rlibc-x1.toml
  rlibc-x2.toml
  glibc-dynamic.toml

apps/xyz/
  tspec/
    config.toml                     # Compat/incompat lists + local mods
  src/
  Cargo.toml

target/
  musl-static-{hash}/               # Isolated by spec name + resolved hash
  rlibc-x2-{hash}/
```

### Local Config Schema

```toml
# apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml

compat = ["musl-static", "rlibc-x2"]      # allowlist (optional)
incompat = ["glibc-dynamic"]              # blocklist (optional)

[mods.musl-static]                        # local modifications (optional)
[mods.musl-static.linker.args]
add = ["-Wl,--gc-sections"]
remove = ["-Wl,--build-id"]
```

### Compatibility Logic

- No `tspec/config.toml` → all specs assumed compatible (optimistic default)
- `incompat = [...]` → blocklist, skip these
- `compat = [...]` → allowlist, only these (once curating)
- Both → compat minus incompat

### Target Directory Naming

Format: `{spec-name}-{hash}`

- Hash is computed from the fully resolved spec (global + local mods)
- Same hash suffix = identical resolved config (user can see redundancy)
- Different hash = different config, isolated builds

Example:
```
target/
  musl-static-abc123de/           # original
  musl-experimental-abc123de/     # same hash! user sees they're identical
  musl-tweaked-77889900/          # different hash, actually different
```

### Spec Resolution Flow

```
global:musl-static.toml
        ↓
  + apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml [mods.musl-static] (if exists)
        ↓
  = resolved spec
        ↓
  hash(resolved) → abc123de
        ↓
  --target-dir=target/musl-static-abc123de
```

## Commands

```bash
cargo xt build xyz -t musl-static         # build with spec
cargo xt build xyz -t all                 # all compatible specs
cargo xt run xyz -t musl-static           # build + run (skip if incompat)
cargo xt compat xyz                       # show compat state
cargo xt compat xyz musl-static           # add to compat list
cargo xt incompat xyz glibc-dynamic       # add to incompat list
cargo xt spec list                        # list global specs
cargo xt spec show musl-static            # show global spec
cargo xt spec show musl-static --crate xyz  # show resolved spec with local mods
cargo xt spec hash musl-static --crate xyz  # show hash
```

All commands explicit (no auto-inference from last build - can relax later).

## Parameter Specification Design

### Philosophy

- Leverage Rust's type system to prevent mistakes at compile time where possible
- Mutually exclusive params = single enum (can't have Release + Debug)
- Tool-specific params = separate types (can't pass linker args to rustc)
- Ordering preserved via Vec (reproducibility)
- Validation at load time for constraints that can't be compile-time enforced

### Type Structure

```rust
// Mutually exclusive choices are enums
enum Profile { Debug, Release }
enum OptLevel { O0, O1, O2, O3, Os, Oz }
enum PanicStrategy { Abort, Unwind }

// Each tool's params as enum variants
enum CargoParam {
    Profile(Profile),
    TargetTriple(String),
    TargetJson(PathBuf),
}

enum RustcParam {
    OptLevel(OptLevel),
    Panic(PanicStrategy),
    Lto(bool),
    CodegenUnits(u32),
    BuildStd(Vec<String>),
    Flag(String),
}

enum LinkerParam {
    Static,
    NoStdlib,
    Entry(String),
    GcSections,
    Arg(String),
}

// Spec is ordered Vecs - order preserved, serialization deterministic
struct Spec {
    cargo: Vec<CargoParam>,
    rustc: Vec<RustcParam>,
    linker: Vec<LinkerParam>,
}
```

### Arg Generation

```rust
trait ToArgs {
    fn to_args(&self) -> Vec<String>;
}

impl ToArgs for LinkerParam {
    fn to_args(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        match self {
            LinkerParam::Static => vec!["-static".into()],
            LinkerParam::Entry(e) => vec![format!("-e{e}")],
            LinkerParam::GcSections => vec!["-Wl,--gc-sections".into()],
            LinkerParam::Arg(s) => vec![s.clone()],
            // ...
        }
    }
}
```

### Validation

At construction/load time, validate:
- At most one Profile in cargo params
- At most one OptLevel in rustc params
- At most one Panic in rustc params
- etc.

Tradeoff: lose some compile-time exclusivity for single-choice params, but gain guaranteed iteration order and simpler mental model.

### Reproducibility

Critical for fair comparisons and consistent hashing:

1. Vec preserves insertion order
2. BTreeMap for any maps (not HashMap)
3. Serde serializes struct fields in definition order
4. Generation methods process in defined sequence

Same spec → same hash → same target dir → reproducible builds.

## Auto-generating Parameters

Potential to bootstrap enum definitions from tool help output:

```bash
rustc -C help          # lists all -C (codegen) options with types
rustc -Z help          # lists all -Z (unstable/nightly) options
cargo build --help     # cargo options
ld --help              # linker options
```

`rustc -C help` output is structured enough to parse:
```
-C opt-level=val       -- optimize with possible levels 0-3, s, or z
-C panic=val           -- panic strategy to compile crate with
-C lto=val             -- perform LLVM link-time optimizations
```

Could parse to generate initial enums, then manually curate for exclusivity rules.

## Open Questions

- Global spec TOML schema (how params serialize to/from TOML)
- How nightly-only features are flagged/validated
- Whether notes/ should capture rotating build logs
- Migration path from existing xtask-based workflow

# xt Design Notes

Design exploration for `xt` - a translation spec based build system to replace/complement `xtask`.

## Goals

- Compare different target triples and compile/linker commands across multiple apps
- Reproducible builds with fair comparisons
- Explore possibilities by trying specs and recording results
- Type-safe parameter specification leveraging Rust's type system

## Core Concepts

### Translation Specs (tspec)

Two-level specification system:

1. **Global specs** (`tspec/*.toml`) - Define compilation strategies
2. **Local config** (`<crate>/tspec/config.toml`) - Crate compatibility and local modifications

### Directory Structure

```
tspec/                              # Global translation specs
  musl-static.toml
  rlibc-x1.toml
  rlibc-x2.toml
  glibc-dynamic.toml

apps/xyz/
  tspec/
    config.toml                     # Compat/incompat lists + local mods
  src/
  Cargo.toml

target/
  musl-static-{hash}/               # Isolated by spec name + resolved hash
  rlibc-x2-{hash}/
```

### Local Config Schema

```toml
# apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml

compat = ["musl-static", "rlibc-x2"]      # allowlist (optional)
incompat = ["glibc-dynamic"]              # blocklist (optional)

[mods.musl-static]                        # local modifications (optional)
[mods.musl-static.linker.args]
add = ["-Wl,--gc-sections"]
remove = ["-Wl,--build-id"]
```

### Compatibility Logic

- No `tspec/config.toml` → all specs assumed compatible (optimistic default)
- `incompat = [...]` → blocklist, skip these
- `compat = [...]` → allowlist, only these (once curating)
- Both → compat minus incompat

### Target Directory Naming

Format: `{spec-name}-{hash}`

- Hash is computed from the fully resolved spec (global + local mods)
- Same hash suffix = identical resolved config (user can see redundancy)
- Different hash = different config, isolated builds

  musl-static-abc123de/           # original
  musl-experimental-abc123de/     # same hash! user sees they're identical
  musl-tweaked-77889900/          # different hash, actually different
```

```
global:musl-static.toml

  + apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml [mods.musl-static] (if exists)

        ↓
  hash(resolved) → abc123de

```

# xt Design Notes

Design exploration for `xt` - a translation spec based build system to replace/complement `xtask`.

## Goals

- Compare different target triples and compile/linker commands across multiple apps
- Reproducible builds with fair comparisons
- Explore possibilities by trying specs and recording results
- Type-safe parameter specification leveraging Rust's type system

## Core Concepts

### Translation Specs (tspec)

Two-level specification system:

1. **Global specs** (`tspec/*.toml`) - Define compilation strategies
2. **Local config** (`<crate>/tspec/config.toml`) - Crate compatibility and local modifications

### Directory Structure

```
tspec/                              # Global translation specs
  musl-static.toml
  rlibc-x1.toml
  rlibc-x2.toml
  glibc-dynamic.toml

apps/xyz/
  tspec/
    config.toml                     # Compat/incompat lists + local mods
  src/
  Cargo.toml

target/
  musl-static-{hash}/               # Isolated by spec name + resolved hash
  rlibc-x2-{hash}/
```

### Local Config Schema

```toml
# apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml

compat = ["musl-static", "rlibc-x2"]      # allowlist (optional)
incompat = ["glibc-dynamic"]              # blocklist (optional)

[mods.musl-static]                        # local modifications (optional)
[mods.musl-static.linker.args]
add = ["-Wl,--gc-sections"]
remove = ["-Wl,--build-id"]
```

### Compatibility Logic

- No `tspec/config.toml` → all specs assumed compatible (optimistic default)
- `incompat = [...]` → blocklist, skip these
- `compat = [...]` → allowlist, only these (once curating)
- Both → compat minus incompat

### Target Directory Naming

Format: `{spec-name}-{hash}`

- Hash is computed from the fully resolved spec (global + local mods)
- Same hash suffix = identical resolved config (user can see redundancy)
- Different hash = different config, isolated builds

Example:
```
target/
  musl-static-abc123de/           # original
  musl-experimental-abc123de/     # same hash! user sees they're identical
  musl-tweaked-77889900/          # different hash, actually different
```

### Spec Resolution Flow

```
global:musl-static.toml
        ↓
  + apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml [mods.musl-static] (if exists)
        ↓
  = resolved spec
        ↓
  hash(resolved) → abc123de
        ↓
  --target-dir=target/musl-static-abc123de
```

## Commands

```bash
cargo xt build xyz -t musl-static         # build with spec
cargo xt build xyz -t all                 # all compatible specs
cargo xt run xyz -t musl-static           # build + run (skip if incompat)
cargo xt compat xyz                       # show compat state
cargo xt compat xyz musl-static           # add to compat list
cargo xt incompat xyz glibc-dynamic       # add to incompat list
cargo xt spec list                        # list global specs
cargo xt spec show musl-static            # show global spec
cargo xt spec show musl-static --crate xyz  # show resolved spec with local mods
cargo xt spec hash musl-static --crate xyz  # show hash
```

All commands explicit (no auto-inference from last build - can relax later).

## Parameter Specification Design

### Philosophy

- Leverage Rust's type system to prevent mistakes at compile time where possible
- Mutually exclusive params = single enum (can't have Release + Debug)
- Tool-specific params = separate types (can't pass linker args to rustc)
- Ordering preserved via Vec (reproducibility)
- Validation at load time for constraints that can't be compile-time enforced

### Type Structure

```rust
// Mutually exclusive choices are enums
enum Profile { Debug, Release }
enum OptLevel { O0, O1, O2, O3, Os, Oz }
enum PanicStrategy { Abort, Unwind }

// Each tool's params as enum variants
enum CargoParam {
    Profile(Profile),
    TargetTriple(String),
    TargetJson(PathBuf),
}

enum RustcParam {
    OptLevel(OptLevel),
    Panic(PanicStrategy),
    Lto(bool),
    CodegenUnits(u32),
    BuildStd(Vec<String>),
    Flag(String),
}

enum LinkerParam {
    Static,
    NoStdlib,
    Entry(String),
    GcSections,
    Arg(String),
}

// Spec is ordered Vecs - order preserved, serialization deterministic
struct Spec {
    cargo: Vec<CargoParam>,
    rustc: Vec<RustcParam>,
    linker: Vec<LinkerParam>,
}
```

### Arg Generation

```rust
trait ToArgs {
    fn to_args(&self) -> Vec<String>;
}

impl ToArgs for LinkerParam {
    fn to_args(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        match self {
            LinkerParam::Static => vec!["-static".into()],
            LinkerParam::Entry(e) => vec![format!("-e{e}")],
            LinkerParam::GcSections => vec!["-Wl,--gc-sections".into()],
            LinkerParam::Arg(s) => vec![s.clone()],
            // ...
        }
    }
}
```

### Validation

At construction/load time, validate:
- At most one Profile in cargo params
- At most one OptLevel in rustc params
- At most one Panic in rustc params
- etc.

Tradeoff: lose some compile-time exclusivity for single-choice params, but gain guaranteed iteration order and simpler mental model.

### Reproducibility

Critical for fair comparisons and consistent hashing:

1. Vec preserves insertion order
2. BTreeMap for any maps (not HashMap)
3. Serde serializes struct fields in definition order
4. Generation methods process in defined sequence

Same spec → same hash → same target dir → reproducible builds.

## Auto-generating Parameters

Potential to bootstrap enum definitions from tool help output:

```bash
rustc -C help          # lists all -C (codegen) options with types
rustc -Z help          # lists all -Z (unstable/nightly) options
cargo build --help     # cargo options
ld --help              # linker options
```

`rustc -C help` output is structured enough to parse:
```
-C opt-level=val       -- optimize with possible levels 0-3, s, or z
-C panic=val           -- panic strategy to compile crate with
-C lto=val             -- perform LLVM link-time optimizations
```

Could parse to generate initial enums, then manually curate for exclusivity rules.

## Open Questions

- Global spec TOML schema (how params serialize to/from TOML)
- How nightly-only features are flagged/validated
- Whether notes/ should capture rotating build logs
- Migration path from existing xtask-based workflow

- Use cargo profiles for opt-level, lto, panic, etc.

# xt Design Notes

Design exploration for `xt` - a translation spec based build system to replace/complement `xtask`.

## Goals

- Compare different target triples and compile/linker commands across multiple apps
- Reproducible builds with fair comparisons
- Explore possibilities by trying specs and recording results
- Type-safe parameter specification leveraging Rust's type system

## Core Concepts

### Translation Specs (tspec)

Two-level specification system:

1. **Global specs** (`tspec/*.toml`) - Define compilation strategies
2. **Local config** (`<crate>/tspec/config.toml`) - Crate compatibility and local modifications

### Directory Structure

```
tspec/                              # Global translation specs
  musl-static.toml
  rlibc-x1.toml
  rlibc-x2.toml
  glibc-dynamic.toml

apps/xyz/
  tspec/
    config.toml                     # Compat/incompat lists + local mods
  src/
  Cargo.toml

target/
  musl-static-{hash}/               # Isolated by spec name + resolved hash
  rlibc-x2-{hash}/
```

### Local Config Schema

```toml
# apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml

compat = ["musl-static", "rlibc-x2"]      # allowlist (optional)
incompat = ["glibc-dynamic"]              # blocklist (optional)

[mods.musl-static]                        # local modifications (optional)
[mods.musl-static.linker.args]
add = ["-Wl,--gc-sections"]
remove = ["-Wl,--build-id"]
```

### Compatibility Logic

- No `tspec/config.toml` → all specs assumed compatible (optimistic default)
- `incompat = [...]` → blocklist, skip these
- `compat = [...]` → allowlist, only these (once curating)
- Both → compat minus incompat

### Target Directory Naming

Format: `{spec-name}-{hash}`

- Hash is computed from the fully resolved spec (global + local mods)
- Same hash suffix = identical resolved config (user can see redundancy)
- Different hash = different config, isolated builds

Example:
```
target/
  musl-static-abc123de/           # original
  musl-experimental-abc123de/     # same hash! user sees they're identical
  musl-tweaked-77889900/          # different hash, actually different
```

### Spec Resolution Flow

```
global:musl-static.toml
        ↓
  + apps/xyz/tspec/config.toml [mods.musl-static] (if exists)
        ↓
  = resolved spec
        ↓
  hash(resolved) → abc123de
        ↓
  --target-dir=target/musl-static-abc123de
```

## Commands

```bash
cargo xt build xyz -t musl-static         # build with spec
cargo xt build xyz -t all                 # all compatible specs
cargo xt run xyz -t musl-static           # build + run (skip if incompat)
cargo xt compat xyz                       # show compat state
cargo xt compat xyz musl-static           # add to compat list
cargo xt incompat xyz glibc-dynamic       # add to incompat list
cargo xt spec list                        # list global specs
cargo xt spec show musl-static            # show global spec
cargo xt spec show musl-static --crate xyz  # show resolved spec with local mods
cargo xt spec hash musl-static --crate xyz  # show hash
```

All commands explicit (no auto-inference from last build - can relax later).

## Parameter Specification Design

### Philosophy

- Leverage Rust's type system to prevent mistakes at compile time where possible
- Mutually exclusive params = single enum (can't have Release + Debug)
- Tool-specific params = separate types (can't pass linker args to rustc)
- Ordering preserved via Vec (reproducibility)
- Validation at load time for constraints that can't be compile-time enforced

### Type Structure

```rust
// Mutually exclusive choices are enums
enum Profile { Debug, Release }
enum OptLevel { O0, O1, O2, O3, Os, Oz }
enum PanicStrategy { Abort, Unwind }

// Each tool's params as enum variants
enum CargoParam {
    Profile(Profile),
    TargetTriple(String),
    TargetJson(PathBuf),
}

enum RustcParam {
    OptLevel(OptLevel),
    Panic(PanicStrategy),
    Lto(bool),
    CodegenUnits(u32),
    BuildStd(Vec<String>),
    Flag(String),
}

enum LinkerParam {
    Static,
    NoStdlib,
    Entry(String),
    GcSections,
    Arg(String),
}

// Spec is ordered Vecs - order preserved, serialization deterministic
struct Spec {
    cargo: Vec<CargoParam>,
    rustc: Vec<RustcParam>,
    linker: Vec<LinkerParam>,
}
```

### Arg Generation

```rust
trait ToArgs {
    fn to_args(&self) -> Vec<String>;
}

impl ToArgs for LinkerParam {
    fn to_args(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        match self {
            LinkerParam::Static => vec!["-static".into()],
            LinkerParam::Entry(e) => vec![format!("-e{e}")],
            LinkerParam::GcSections => vec!["-Wl,--gc-sections".into()],
            LinkerParam::Arg(s) => vec![s.clone()],
            // ...
        }
    }
}
```

### Validation

At construction/load time, validate:
- At most one Profile in cargo params
- At most one OptLevel in rustc params
- At most one Panic in rustc params
- etc.

Tradeoff: lose some compile-time exclusivity for single-choice params, but gain guaranteed iteration order and simpler mental model.

### Reproducibility

Critical for fair comparisons and consistent hashing:

1. Vec preserves insertion order
2. BTreeMap for any maps (not HashMap)
3. Serde serializes struct fields in definition order
4. Generation methods process in defined sequence

Same spec → same hash → same target dir → reproducible builds.

## Auto-generating Parameters

Potential to bootstrap enum definitions from tool help output:

```bash
rustc -C help          # lists all -C (codegen) options with types
rustc -Z help          # lists all -Z (unstable/nightly) options
cargo build --help     # cargo options
ld --help              # linker options
```

`rustc -C help` output is structured enough to parse:
```
-C opt-level=val       -- optimize with possible levels 0-3, s, or z
-C panic=val           -- panic strategy to compile crate with
-C lto=val             -- perform LLVM link-time optimizations
```

Could parse to generate initial enums, then manually curate for exclusivity rules.

## Open Questions

- Global spec TOML schema (how params serialize to/from TOML)
- How nightly-only features are flagged/validated
- Whether notes/ should capture rotating build logs
- Migration path from existing xtask-based workflow

1→# rlibc-x
     2→
     3→A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→## Goals
     6→
     7→- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
     8→- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
     9→- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`
    10→
    11→## Results
    12→
    13→The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:
    14→
    15→```
    16→$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
    17→-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1
    18→
    19→$ file target/release/ex-x1
    20→ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
    21→```
    22→
    23→This is achieved through:
    24→- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
    25→- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
    26→- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
    27→- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
    28→- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols
    29→
    30→For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces **~6 KB** with `-opt` (nightly).
    31→
    32→See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison.
    33→
    34→## Workspace Structure
    35→
    36→| Directory | Description |
    37→|-----------|-------------|
    38→| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
    39→| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~6-41 KB binaries) |
    40→| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
    41→| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`, `func-analysis`) |
    42→| [notes/](notes/) | Technical notes and findings |
    43→| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |
    44→
    45→## Two Approaches
    46→
    47→**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.
    48→
    49→**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.
    50→
    51→## Optimized Builds
    52→
    53→The `-opt` flag dramatically reduces binary sizes by eliminating Rust's panic formatting machinery:
    54→
    55→```bash
    56→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -opt -s     # ~6 KB (vs ~41 KB)
    57→cargo xtask build ex-glibc -r -opt -s  # ~9 KB (vs ~298 KB)
    58→cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt -s   # ~23 KB (vs ~381 KB)
    59→```
    60→
    61→See [notes/opt-notes.md](notes/opt-notes.md) for details.
    62→
    63→## Quick Start
    64→
    65→```bash
    66→# Build and run
    67→cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
    68→cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2
    69→
    70→# Test
    71→cargo xtask test               # run all tests
    72→cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode
    73→
    74→# Build release
    75→cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
    76→```
    77→
    78→For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)
    79→
    80→## Verifying No libc Usage
    81→
    82→The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:
    83→
    84→```bash
    85→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
    86→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
    87→```
    88→
    89→All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.
    90→
    91→## Status
    92→
    93→This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:
    94→
    95→- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
    96→- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust
    97→
    98→## Origin
    99→
   100→Started with this prompt for Claude Code:
   101→
   102→> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces **~6 KB** with `-opt` (nightly).

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~6-41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`, `func-analysis`) |
| [notes/](notes/) | Technical notes and findings |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Optimized Builds

The `-opt` flag dramatically reduces binary sizes by eliminating Rust's panic formatting machinery:

```bash
cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -opt -s     # ~6 KB (vs ~41 KB)
cargo xtask build ex-glibc -r -opt -s  # ~9 KB (vs ~298 KB)
cargo xtask build ex-musl -r -opt -s   # ~23 KB (vs ~381 KB)
```

See [notes/opt-notes.md](notes/opt-notes.md) for details.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# rlibc-x1

A minimal `#![no_std]` runtime for Rust on Linux x86_64.

Produces tiny binaries (~1.4 KB) by eliminating standard library overhead entirely.

## How It Works

```
_start (asm) → _start_rust() → main() → exit()
```

- **`_start`** - Assembly entry point, sets up stack and calls `_start_rust()`
- **`_start_rust()`** - Calls user's `main()` function
- **`main()`** - User-defined, must call `exit()` to terminate
- **`exit()`** - Direct syscall, no glibc

## Provided Functions

| Category | Functions |
|----------|-----------|
| Process | `exit()` |
| Memory | `malloc()`, `realloc()`, `free()` (no-op) |
| I/O | `read()`, `write()` |
| Syscalls | `syscall0` through `syscall6` |

The allocator is a simple bump allocator using `brk()`. Memory is never freed.

## Usage

1. Add dependency:
   ```toml
   [dependencies]
   rlibc-x1 = { path = "../rlibc-x1" }
   ```

2. Configure your app:
   ```rust
   #![no_std]
   #![no_main]

   #[unsafe(no_mangle)]
   fn main() {
       rlibc_x1::exit(0);
   }
   ```

3. Add linker flags in `build.rs`:
   ```rust
   fn main() {
       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-nostartfiles");
       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-static");
   }
   ```

## Example

See [apps/ex-x1](../apps/ex-x1) and [apps/hw-x1](../apps/hw-x1) for complete examples.

1→# rlibc-x2
     2→
     3→A libc replacement that allows using Rust's standard library without linking to glibc.
     4→
     5→Produces statically-linked binaries that use `std` but make no glibc calls:
     6→- **~41 KB** with stable Rust
     7→- **~6 KB** with nightly optimizations
     8→
     9→## How It Works
    10→
    11→```
    12→_start (asm) → __libc_start_main() → Rust's main → user's main()
    13→```
    14→
    15→- **`_start`** - Assembly entry point
    16→- **`__libc_start_main()`** - Initializes TLS, environment, then calls Rust's generated main
    17→- **Rust's main** - Standard library initialization
    18→- **User's `main()`** - Normal Rust main function
    19→
    20→## Provided Symbols
    21→
    22→| Category | Symbols |
    23→|----------|---------|
    24→| Process | `_start`, `__libc_start_main`, `exit`, `abort`, `__libc_stack_end` |
    25→| Environment | `environ`, `getenv` |
    26→| Memory | `malloc`, `realloc`, `calloc`, `free`, `memcpy`, `memset`, `memmove`, `memcmp` |
    27→| I/O | `read`, `write`, `writev` |
    28→| Threading | `pthread_*` stubs, TLS initialization |
    29→| Other | `__errno_location`, signal stubs |
    30→
    31→## Usage
    32→
    33→1. Add dependency:
    34→   ```toml
    35→   [dependencies]
    36→   rlibc-x2 = { path = "../rlibc-x2" }
    37→   ```
    38→
    39→2. Force linking in your app:
    40→   ```rust
    41→   extern crate rlibc_x2;
    42→
    43→   fn main() {
    44→       std::process::exit(42);
    45→   }
    46→   ```
    47→
    48→3. Add linker flags in `build.rs`:
    49→   ```rust
    50→   fn main() {
    51→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-static");
    52→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-nostdlib");
    53→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-nodefaultlibs");
    54→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-e_start");
    55→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-Wl,--undefined=_start");
    56→       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg-bin=myapp=-Wl,--undefined=__libc_start_main");
    57→   }
    58→   ```
    59→
    60→## The "Dynamically Linked" Discrepancy
    61→
    62→`file` reports "dynamically linked" but `ldd` says "statically linked" - both are correct:
    63→
    64→- **`file`** sees `.dynamic` and `.dynsym` ELF sections (required by Rust's std)
    65→- **`ldd`** sees no INTERP section, so no dynamic linker is invoked
    66→
    67→Use `strace` to verify - only ~7 syscalls, no library loading.
    68→
    69→## Integration Tests
    70→
    71→Tests are in `tests/` and built as separate binaries:
    72→
    73→```bash
    74→cargo xtask test rlibc-x2    # runs rlibc-x2-tests binaries
    75→```
    76→
    77→## Build Modes
    78→
    79→### Stable (default)
    80→
    81→Works with stable Rust, produces ~41 KB binaries:
    82→
    83→```bash
    84→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -s
    85→```
    86→
    87→### Optimized (nightly)
    88→
    89→Uses nightly features for ~6 KB binaries:
    90→
    91→```bash
    92→cargo xtask build ex-x2 -r -opt -s
    93→```
    94→
    95→The `-opt` flag enables:
    96→- `-Z build-std` - Rebuild std from source for better LTO
    97→- `-Z panic-immediate-abort` - Eliminate panic formatting code
    98→- Linker version script - Enable dead code elimination
    99→- Custom target - `x86_64-unknown-linux-rlibcx2.json`
   100→
